templates.wajadtu: I found it in the writing of {name}

term_why.'an: Does not say how it was received ('an'ana). Counted as connected when the two narrators could have met and the narrator is not known for concealing a gap (tadlis).
term_why.akhbarana: Many critics used it for a text read back to the teacher ('ard); others as haddathana.
term_why.anba'ana: Later scholars often used it for transmission by permission (ijaza).
term_why.balagha: The narrator says only that it reached him from that man: who brought it to him is not named (a balagh).
term_why.bare: The compiler names his teacher without a term, as al-Kulayni does: it is his own transmission from that teacher.
term_why.haddathana: The teacher recited it to a group that included the narrator: heard directly.
term_why.haddathani: The teacher recited it to the narrator alone: heard directly.
term_why.kataba: The teacher wrote it to the narrator (mukataba): accepted by most critics, though not heard.
term_why.qala: Cited without saying how it was received (ta'liq): the compiler or a narrator quotes him, as al-Bukhari does after a tahwil ("وقال ابن وهب").
term_why.qara'tu 'ala: The narrator read the text back to the teacher ('ard).
term_why.quri'a 'ala: The text was read back to the teacher while the narrator listened.
term_why.sa'ala: The narrator asked him and heard the answer from him: heard directly.
term_why.sa'altu: The narrator asked him and heard the answer from him: heard directly.
term_why.sami'a: Reports that the narrator heard it directly.
term_why.su'ila: He was asked, and the narrator reports his answer; how the narrator received it is not said.
term_why.wajadtu: The narrator found it in the teacher's writing (wijada), without hearing it from him: a weaker way of receiving.
term_why.za'ama: Reports a statement; says nothing about how it was received.

book_marks.تمييز: no narration in these books; named to tell him apart

compiler: A scholar who gathered hadith into a book, each with the chain he heard it through. The first link of every chain is his own teacher; the last is usually the Companion who heard the Prophet.
critic: A scholar who judged the narrators themselves — their honesty and the accuracy of their memory — in fixed words that rank them, from Companion down to liar (Ibn Hajar uses twelve ranks).
grader: A scholar who judged each hadith of a book: sahih (sound), hasan (good), da'if (weak), and so on. Different scholars can judge the same hadith differently; comparing them shows how strict each one is.
